claim: RIF1 mutants that block Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) binding activated telomeric origins but did not elongate telomeres.
source: We found that RIF1 mutants that block Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) binding activated telomeric origins but did not elongate telomeres.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overexpression of ∆N-Dbf4 and Cdc7 increased DDK activity and activated telomeric origins, yet telomere length was unchanged.
source: In a second approach, we found overexpression of ∆N-Dbf4 and Cdc7 increased DDK activity and activated telomeric origins, yet telomere length was unchanged.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The sld3-A mcm5-bob1 mutant that de-regulates the pre-replication complex showed no change in telomere length despite activating origins.
source: We tested a third mechanism to activate origins using the sld3-A mcm5-bob1 mutant that de-regulates the pre-replication complex, and again saw no change in telomere length.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neither rif1-∆1322 nor rif1HOOK affected firing of telomeric origins.
source: We found that neither rif1-∆1322 nor rif1HOOK affected firing of telomeric origins.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Telomeric origin firing does not cause telomere elongation.
source: We conclude that telomeric origin firing does not cause telomere elongation, and the role of Rif1 in regulating origin firing is separable from its role in regulating telomere length.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental approaches showing that origin firing and telomere length are uncoupled.

claim: The role of Rif1 in regulating origin firing is separable from its role in regulating telomere length.
source: We conclude that telomeric origin firing does not cause telomere elongation, and the role of Rif1 in regulating origin firing is separable from its role in regulating telomere length.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental approaches showing that origin firing and telomere length are uncoupled.

claim: Telomeres consist of tandem repeats of simple G- and T-rich sequences at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes.
source: They consist of tandem repeats of simple G- and T-rich sequences at the ends of eukaryotic chromosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about telomere structure.

claim: Telomeres shorten with repeated rounds of DNA replication.
source: Telomeres shorten with repeated rounds of DNA replication, and this shortening is counterbalanced by the enzyme telomerase (Greider and Blackburn, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Greider and Blackburn, 1985.

claim: Telomere shortening is counterbalanced by the enzyme telomerase.
source: Telomeres shorten with repeated rounds of DNA replication, and this shortening is counterbalanced by the enzyme telomerase (Greider and Blackburn, 1985).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Greider and Blackburn, 1985.

claim: Telomere lengths differ between species, but in all healthy cells, length is maintained within a defined length distribution.
source: Telomere lengths differ between species, but, in all healthy cells, length is maintained within a defined length distribution (Greider, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Greider, 1996.

claim: Short telomeres signal a DNA damage response that limits cell division.
source: Yet the maintenance of the length distribution is crucial, as short telomeres signal a DNA damage response that limits cell division (d'Adda di Fagagna et al., 2003; Enomoto et al., 2002; Hemann et al., 2001; IJpma and Greider, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In human patients with defective telomere maintenance, short telomere syndromes manifest as degenerative diseases, including bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis.
source: In human patients with defective telomere maintenance, short telomere syndromes manifest as degenerative diseases, including bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis (Armanios and Blackburn, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Armanios and Blackburn, 2012.

claim: Inappropriate telomere lengthening can contribute to immortalization of cancer cells.
source: Conversely, inappropriate telomere lengthening can contribute to immortalization of cancer cells (Autexier and Greider, 1996; Greider, 1990) and to a predisposition to cancer (McNally et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Autexier and Greider, 1996 and Greider, 1990.

claim: Inappropriate telomere lengthening can contribute to a predisposition to cancer.
source: Conversely, inappropriate telomere lengthening can contribute to immortalization of cancer cells (Autexier and Greider, 1996; Greider, 1990) and to a predisposition to cancer (McNally et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McNally et al., 2019.

claim: Telomere elongation in yeast only occurs after passage of a replication fork.
source: Telomere elongation in yeast only occurs after passage of a replication fork (Dionne and Wellinger, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dionne and Wellinger, 1998.

claim: Mutations in components of the replication fork alter telomere length in yeast.
source: Mutations in components of the replication fork alter telomere length in yeast; for example, components of lagging strand synthesis such as DNA polymerase α, RFC, Dna2, and Fen1, cause telomere elongation (reviewed in Greider, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review by Greider, 2016.

claim: DNA polymerases α and δ and DNA primase are all essential for de novo telomere addition by telomerase.
source: Further, DNA polymerases α and δ and DNA primase are all essential for de novo telomere addition by telomerase (Diede and Gottschling, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Diede and Gottschling, 1999.

claim: The canonical yeast single-strand telomere end-binding complex, Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1, is considered a telomere-specific Replication Protein A (t-RPA).
source: The canonical yeast single-strand telomere end-binding complex, Cdc13/Stn1/Ten1, is considered a telomere-specific Replication Protein A (t-RPA) (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2007.

claim: t-RPA interacts directly with DNA polymerase α and has been proposed to assist DNA replication through telomere repeats.
source: t-RPA interacts directly with DNA polymerase α and has been proposed to assist DNA replication through telomere repeats, which further links telomere length and DNA replication (Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2010.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, deletion of RIF1 leads to extensive telomere elongation.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, deletion of RIF1 leads to extensive telomere elongation (Hardy et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hardy et al., 1992.

claim: The role of Rif1 in regulating telomere length is conserved in distantly related yeast such as Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Candida glabrata.
source: This role of Rif1 in regulating telomere length is conserved in distantly related yeast such as Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001) and Candida glabrata (Castaño et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001 and Castaño et al., 2005.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Rif1 binds to telomeres through its interaction with the telomere-specific double-stranded DNA binding protein Rap1.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Rif1 binds to telomeres through its interaction with the telomere-specific double-stranded DNA binding protein Rap1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rif1 function in S. cerevisiae.

claim: Telomeric origins fire late in S phase.
source: Evidence that Rif1 regulates telomeric origin firing (Cornacchia et al., 2012; Davé et al., 2014; Hayano et al., 2012; Peace et al., 2014; Yamazaki et al., 2012) helped explain the longstanding observation that telomeric origins fire late in S phase.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transplanting an origin sequence, which is known to fire early at its endogenous locus, to a telomere, caused that origin to instead fire late.
source: Transplanting an origin sequence, which is known to fire early at its endogenous locus, to a telomere, caused that origin to instead fire late (Ferguson et al., 1991; Ferguson and Fangman, 1992; Wellinger et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 1991, Ferguson and Fangman, 1992, and Wellinger et al., 1993.

claim: Cell synchronization showed that telomeres incorporate BrdU late in S phase.
source: Further, cell synchronization showed that telomeres incorporate BrdU late in S phase (Raghuraman et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raghuraman et al., 2001.

claim: Rif1 binding to telomeres represses nearby origin firing.
source: Rif1 binding to telomeres and repressing nearby origin firing (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014; Peace et al., 2014) presented a nice explanation for the late replication of telomeric origins.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014, Hiraga et al., 2014, Mattarocci et al., 2014, and Peace et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanism of Rif1 repression of origin firing works through its interaction with Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1, GLC7 in S. cerevisiae).
source: Several groups showed that the mechanism of Rif1 repression of origin firing works through its interaction with Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1, GLC7 in S. cerevisiae).
evidence: This statement is supported by the context and citations in the following sentences.

claim: PP1 can dephosphorylate key substrates in the pre-replication complex (Pre-RC) including Mcm4.
source: PP1 can dephosphorylate key substrates in the pre-replication complex (Pre-RC) including Mcm4 (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014) and thus block origin activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014, Hiraga et al., 2014, and Mattarocci et al., 2014.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 is required for origin activation at the initiation of S phase.
source: DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 is required for origin activation at the initiation of S phase, so PP1 antagonizes DDK phosphorylation to block origin firing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of DDK in origin activation.

claim: PP1 antagonizes DDK phosphorylation to block origin firing.
source: DDK phosphorylation of Mcm4 is required for origin activation at the initiation of S phase, so PP1 antagonizes DDK phosphorylation to block origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposing roles of DDK and PP1 in Mcm4 phosphorylation.

claim: Rif1 recruitment of PP1 to repress origin firing is highly conserved across species including S. pombe, Drosophila, and mammalian cells.
source: Rif1 recruitment of PP1 to repress origin firing is highly conserved across species including S. pombe, Drosophila, and mammalian cells, although the PP1 interaction motifs, RVxF and SILK, are located in a different region of the protein in mammalian cells (Sreesankar et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sreesankar et al., 2012 and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: The PP1 interaction motifs, RVxF and SILK, are located in a different region of the protein in mammalian cells compared to yeast.
source: Rif1 recruitment of PP1 to repress origin firing is highly conserved across species including S. pombe, Drosophila, and mammalian cells, although the PP1 interaction motifs, RVxF and SILK, are located in a different region of the protein in mammalian cells (Sreesankar et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sreesankar et al., 2012 and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Repressing origin firing is a core function of Rif1.
source: This conservation of function indicates repressing origin firing is a core function of Rif1.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of Rif1's role in origin firing across species.

claim: Deletion of RIF1 activates telomeric origin firing.
source: Deletion of RIF1 activates telomeric origin firing (Davé et al., 2014; Hafner et al., 2018; Mattarocci et al., 2014; Peace et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014, Hafner et al., 2018, Mattarocci et al., 2014, and Peace et al., 2014.

claim: Origin activation by Rif1 deletion requires Rif1 binding to PP1 through canonical binding motifs RVxF and SILK.
source: This origin activation requires Rif1 binding to PP1 through canonical binding motifs RVxF and SILK, (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014, Hiraga et al., 2014, and Mattarocci et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of Mcm4 is increased in rif1∆ and in rif1-PP1 binding site mutants.
source: Others have shown that phosphorylation of Mcm4 is increased in rif1∆ and in rif1-PP1 binding site mutants (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014, Hiraga et al., 2014, and Mattarocci et al., 2014.

claim: rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs showed increased levels of Mcm4 phosphorylation compared to WT in both G1 and S phase.
source: We found rif1∆ and our rif1-pp1bs mutant showed increased levels of Mcm4 phosphorylation compared to WT in both G1 and S phase, as other groups have shown (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lambda phosphatase treatment confirmed that the upper band on the western is due to Mcm4 phosphorylation.
source: Lambda phosphatase treatment confirmed that the upper band on the western is due to Mcm4 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs samples showed increased telomeric origin firing compared to WT at the dormant telomeric origin ARS608 and to a lesser extent at ARS608.5 and ARS609.
source: rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs samples showed increased telomeric origin firing compared to WT at the dormant telomeric origin ARS608 and to a lesser extent at ARS608.5 and ARS609 as expected from previous work.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The nearby early origin ARS607 fired efficiently in all strains (WT, rif1∆, and rif1-pp1bs).
source: In contrast, the nearby early origin ARS607 fired efficiently in all strains (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The left telomeric origins showed slight increase in activation in rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs.
source: Analysis across the entire Chromosome VI showed that the left telomeric origins also showed slight increase in activation in rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There was higher relative copy number at most origins in the rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs mutants, with the majority of the change seen in typically late/inefficient origins.
source: As expected, there was higher relative copy number at most origins in the rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs mutants, with the majority of the change seen in typically late/inefficient origins, demonstrated by a low relative copy number in WT cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs were statistically significantly increased in origin firing compared to WT.
source: To quantify the increase in origin firing, we calculated the difference in relative copy number of origins for rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs to determine the relative fraction of origins fired compared to WT (see Materials and methods) and found both rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs were statistically significantly increased compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Disruption of Rif1 interaction with PP1 leads to origin activation.
source: These results support the previous work (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014), which showed that disruption of Rif1 interaction with PP1 leads to origin activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citations to previous work.

claim: rif1∆ had long telomeres as expected.
source: Southern blots of rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs showed that, while rif1∆ had long telomeres as expected, rif1-pp1bs mutants showed telomere length similar to WT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: rif1-pp1bs mutants showed telomere length similar to WT.
source: Southern blots of rif1∆ and rif1-pp1bs showed that, while rif1∆ had long telomeres as expected, rif1-pp1bs mutants showed telomere length similar to WT (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Passaging the rif1-pp1bs mutants in liquid culture showed no change in telomere length compared to WT, whereas rif1∆ continued to elongate.
source: We passaged the rif1-pp1bs mutants in liquid culture to overcome any phenotypic delay in telomere lengthening and still found no change in telomere length compared to WT, whereas rif1∆ continued to elongate (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The rif1-R/S mutant from Mattarocci et al., 2014 had wildtype telomere length similar to rif1-pp1bs.
source: We generated the previously published RIF1 PP1 binding mutant called rif1-R/S mutant from Mattarocci et al., 2014, and found it had wildtype telomere length similar to our rif1-pp1bs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The rif1-pp1bs and the rif1-R/S proteins were stably expressed.
source: Next, we examined protein stability by western blot and found that that our mutant, rif1-pp1bs, and the rif1-R/S were stably expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Mcm4 phosphorylation levels increased in rif1-pp1bs and rif1-R/S to a similar extent.
source: We also found that Mcm4 phosphorylation levels increased in rif1-pp1bs and rif1-R/S to a similar extent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The rif1-pp1bsD mutant was not stably expressed.
source: In contrast, the RIF1 PP1 binding mutant reported in Hiraga et al., 2014 and further analyzed in Kedziora et al., 2018, rif1-pp1bsD, in which two additional putative PP1 binding sites 3 and 4 were mutated, was not stably expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,F.

claim: The rif1-pp1bs-4 protein was not stably expressed.
source: To further examine the potential stability issues, we mutated the additional sites 3 and 4 in our construct to generate rif1-pp1bs-4 and found this protein was also not stably expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,G.

claim: Mutation of the additional two sites in RIF1 may disrupt protein folding and cause degradation of Rif1 protein.
source: This data suggests that mutation of the additional two sites in RIF1 may disrupt protein folding and cause degradation of Rif1 protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutating sites 3 and 4 leads to protein instability.

claim: The long telomere phenotype seen in Kedziora et al. can be attributed to the absence of Rif1 protein.
source: Therefore, the long telomere phenotype seen in Kedziora et al., (and our unpublished data) can be attributed to the absence of Rif1 protein (Kedziora et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the rif1-pp1bsD mutant has low protein levels and long telomeres.

claim: Mutating the Rif1-PP1 binding site increases telomeric origin firing to a similar extent as a rif1∆, but this increased firing does not result in telomere elongation.
source: We conclude, from our rif1-pp1bs and the Mattarocci et al. rif1-R/S mutant, that mutating the Rif1-PP1 binding site increases telomeric origin firing to a similar extent as a rif1∆, but this increased firing does not result in telomere elongation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that rif1-pp1bs and rif1-R/S increase origin firing but not telomere length.

claim: ∆N-dbf4 levels were stabilized in G1 compared to the levels of full length Dbf4, which is degraded in G1.
source: Western blots showed that ∆N-dbf4 levels were stabilized in G1 compared to the levels of full length Dbf4, which is degraded in G1, as previously shown (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mcm4 phosphorylation was increased in cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4, or both ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7.
source: Mcm4 phosphorylation was increased in cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4, or both ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 (Figure 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4 alone or in combination with Cdc7 showed a robust increase in telomeric ARS608 firing and to a lesser extent ARS608.5 and ARS609 compared to WT.
source: Cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4 alone or in combination with Cdc7 showed a robust increase in telomeric ARS608 firing and to a lesser extent ARS608.5 and ARS609 compared to WT (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Analysis of the entire Chromosome VI showed increased firing at both telomeric and non-telomeric origins with ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 overexpression.
source: Analysis of the entire Chromosome VI showed increased firing at both telomeric and non-telomeric origins with ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 overexpression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of ∆N-dbf4 and also ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 together resulted in higher relative copy number at most origins compared to WT cells, with a dramatic increase in late firing origins.
source: Analysis of relative copy number at each origin showed overexpression of ∆N-dbf4 and also ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 together resulted in higher relative copy number at most origins compared to WT cells, with a dramatic increase in late firing origins (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Overexpression of both ∆N-dbf4 and ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 together showed a significant increase in global origin firing when compared to WT.
source: Overexpression of both ∆N-dbf4 and ∆N-dbf4 and Cdc7 together showed a significant increase in global origin firing when compared to WT, further depicted by heatmap representation of relative copy number spanning 10 kb around the each origin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Despite the strong activation of telomeric origins in cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4 and ∆N-dbf4 with Cdc7, there was no change in telomere length.
source: Despite the strong activation of telomeric origins, and many other origins, in cells overexpressing ∆N-dbf4 and ∆N-dbf4 with Cdc7, we saw no change in telomere length (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Increasing origin activation through DDK overexpression increases origin firing but does not affect telomere length.
source: We conclude that increasing origin activation through DDK overexpression increases origin firing but does not affect telomere length.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that DDK overexpression increases origin firing but not telomere length.

claim: The Diffley lab showed that the double mutant sld3-A mcm5-bob1 activates late origins.
source: The Diffley lab showed that the double mutant sld3-A mcm5-bob1 activates late origins (Zegerman and Diffley, 2007; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Zegerman and Diffley, 2007 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Mcm4 phosphorylation levels increased in sld3-A bob1 double mutants.
source: Mcm4 phosphorylation levels increased in sld3-A bob1 double mutants (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Analysis of origin firing showed a robust increase in origin firing in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT for the dormant, telomeric origins ARS608, ARS608.5 and ARS609.
source: Analysis of origin firing showed a robust increase in origin firing in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT for the dormant, telomeric origins ARS608, ARS608.5 and ARS609 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B relating to Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Examination of all of Chromosome VI showed that most origins increased firing in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT.
source: Examination of all of Chromosome VI showed that most origins increased firing in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The peaks around each origin were narrower in sld3-A bob1 than in WT, which may be due to depletion of the nucleotide pools in HU, decreasing replication fork progression when so many origins are activated at once.
source: The peaks around each origin were narrower in sld3-A bob1 than in WT; this may be due to depletion of the nucleotide pools in HU, decreasing replication fork progression when so many origins are activated at once, as noted in Mantiero et al., 2011.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of narrower peaks and is supported by a citation to Mantiero et al., 2011.

claim: Quantitation of the relative copy number at origins in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT showed a significant increase in origin firing in sld3-A bob1.
source: Quantitation of the relative copy number at origins in sld3-A bob1 compared to WT showed a significant increase in origin firing in sld3-A bob1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Comparison of relative copy number at each origin showed early firing of almost all origins in sld3-A bob1, which is particularly striking at the late WT origins.
source: Comparison of relative copy number at each origin showed early firing of almost all origins, which is particularly striking at the late WT origins (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Despite the robust telomeric origin activation, the sld3-A bob1 double mutant maintained WT telomere length.
source: Remarkably, despite the robust telomeric origin activation, the sld3-A bob1 double mutant maintained WT telomere length (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Passaging WT and sld3-A bob1 cells in liquid culture for 6 days showed that telomere length was maintained at WT length.
source: To examine this further, we passaged WT and sld3-A bob1 cells in liquid culture for 6 days, and telomere length was maintained at WT length (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Increased origin firing in the sld3-A bob1 double mutant does not lead to a change in telomere length.
source: We conclude that increased origin firing in the sld3-A bob1 double mutant does not lead to a change in telomere length.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that sld3-A bob1 increases origin firing but not telomere length.

claim: The rif1-∆1322 and the rif1HOOK proteins were stably expressed.
source: We confirmed by western that the rif1-∆1322 and the rif1HOOK proteins were stably expressed (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rif1-∆1322 had long telomeres, although not as long as rif1∆.
source: rif1-∆1322 had long telomeres, although not as long as rif1∆ (Figure 4B) as noted by Shi et al., 2013, and rif1HOOK showed long telomeres similar to rif1∆ as previously described (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citations to Shi et al., 2013 and Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: rif1HOOK showed long telomeres similar to rif1∆.
source: rif1-∆1322 had long telomeres, although not as long as rif1∆ (Figure 4B) as noted by Shi et al., 2013, and rif1HOOK showed long telomeres similar to rif1∆ as previously described (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: There was no increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation levels in either rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK.
source: We found no increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation levels in either rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The lack of increased Mcm4 phosphorylation suggests that rif1-∆1322 can still recruit PP1 to dephosphorylate Mcm4 even though it cannot localize to the telomere.
source: This lack of increased Mcm4 phosphorylation suggests that rif1-∆1322 can still recruit PP1 to dephosphorylate Mcm4 even though it cannot localize to the telomere.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rif1-∆1322 does not increase Mcm4 phosphorylation despite lacking telomere localization.

claim: Telomeric origins ARS608, ARS608.5, and ARS609 were not activated in either rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK mutants.
source: Telomeric origins ARS608, ARS608.5, and ARS609 were not activated in either rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK mutants, and there was very little change in most origins along the entire Chromosome VI (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Analysis of relative copy number at each origin compared to WT showed no change in origin firing in the rif1HOOK mutant, while rif1-∆1322 showed an apparent small decrease in origin firing.
source: Analysis of relative copy number at each origin compared to WT showed no change in origin firing in the rif1HOOK mutant, while rif1-∆1322 showed an apparent small decrease in origin firing (Figure 4E) as seen previously (Hafner et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and a citation to Hafner et al., 2018.

claim: Quantification of the relative copy number showed no significant increase in origin firing in rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK compared to WT.
source: Quantification of the relative copy number showed no significant increase in origin firing in rif1-∆1322 or rif1HOOK compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A substantial increase in telomere length in rif1HOOK mutant does not alter telomeric origin firing.
source: These data suggest that a substantial increase in telomere length in rif1HOOK mutant does not alter telomeric origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rif1HOOK has long telomeres but no change in origin firing.

claim: Using three unique genetic pathways (Rif1 mutations, DDK overexpression, and bypass mutants in the pre-RC), activating telomeric origins is not sufficient to increase telomere length.
source: We have shown, using three unique genetic pathways: Rif1 mutations, DDK overexpression, and bypass mutants in the pre-RC, that activating telomeric origins is not sufficient to increase telomere length.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: sld3-A bob1 and ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression showed the highest relative activation scores for ARS608, 24.36 and 25.83, respectively.
source: We found that sld3-A bob1 and ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression showed the highest relative activation scores, 24.36 and 25.83, respectively.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: ∆N-dbf4 overexpression alone had an ARS608 activation score of 14.09.
source: ∆N-dbf4 overexpression alone had a score of 14.09, while rif1-pp1bs was 10.15 and rif1∆ was 6.54.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: rif1-pp1bs had an ARS608 activation score of 10.15.
source: ∆N-dbf4 overexpression alone had a score of 14.09, while rif1-pp1bs was 10.15 and rif1∆ was 6.54.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: rif1∆ had an ARS608 activation score of 6.54.
source: ∆N-dbf4 overexpression alone had a score of 14.09, while rif1-pp1bs was 10.15 and rif1∆ was 6.54.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: rif1-∆1322 had a low ARS608 activation score of 1.50.
source: In contrast, rif1-∆1322 and rif1HOOK had low ARS608 scores of 1.50 and 2.33 respectively, but have long telomeres.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: rif1HOOK had a low ARS608 activation score of 2.33.
source: In contrast, rif1-∆1322 and rif1HOOK had low ARS608 scores of 1.50 and 2.33 respectively, but have long telomeres.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of origin firing data.

claim: The two well established functions of Rif1, regulating origin firing and regulating telomere length, represent independent, separable functions of Rif1.
source: Our data indicate that the two well established functions of Rif1, regulating origin firing and regulating telomere length, represent independent, separable functions of Rif1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: PP1 binding to Rif1 regulates origin activation.
source: From our results and the results from Mattarocci et al., 2014, we conclude that PP1 binding to Rif1 regulates origin activation, and our data further indicates this interaction is dispensable for telomere length regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that PP1 binding mutants increase origin firing but not telomere length.

claim: PP1 binding to Rif1 is dispensable for telomere length regulation.
source: From our results and the results from Mattarocci et al., 2014, we conclude that PP1 binding to Rif1 regulates origin activation, and our data further indicates this interaction is dispensable for telomere length regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that PP1 binding mutants increase origin firing but not telomere length.

claim: Several different mechanisms can independently regulate telomeric origin firing.
source: Our results suggest that several different mechanisms can independently regulate telomeric origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different mutants activate origins to different extents.

claim: The deletion of RIF1 caused origin activation in a subset of cells.
source: The deletion of RIF1 caused origin activation in a subset of cells; however, many more cells activated telomeric origins in both ∆N-dbf4 overexpression and in sld3-A bob1 mutants, as indicated by the higher peaks at ARS608, 608.5, and 609 (Figures 1C, 2C and 3B).
evidence: This is based on the observation of peak heights in origin firing data.

claim: Many more cells activated telomeric origins in both ∆N-dbf4 overexpression and in sld3-A bob1 mutants compared to rif1∆.
source: The deletion of RIF1 caused origin activation in a subset of cells; however, many more cells activated telomeric origins in both ∆N-dbf4 overexpression and in sld3-A bob1 mutants, as indicated by the higher peaks at ARS608, 608.5, and 609 (Figures 1C, 2C and 3B).
evidence: This is based on the observation of peak heights in origin firing data shown in Figures 1C, 2C and 3B.

claim: rif1∆ has only a small effect on origin firing.
source: Other groups have also found that rif1∆ has only a small effect on origin firing (Hafner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hafner et al., 2018.

claim: While sld3-A mutants activate some origins, there is an additive effect of mutating both sld3-A and bob1.
source: The Diffley lab showed that, while sld3-A mutants activate some origins, there is an additive effect of mutating both sld3-A and bob1, indicating that independent mechanisms of activation can have an additive effect on origin firing (Sheu et al., 2016; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sheu et al., 2016 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Independent mechanisms of activation can have an additive effect on origin firing.
source: The Diffley lab showed that, while sld3-A mutants activate some origins, there is an additive effect of mutating both sld3-A and bob1, indicating that independent mechanisms of activation can have an additive effect on origin firing (Sheu et al., 2016; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sheu et al., 2016 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: The height of the peak at the origin is linked to the number of cells that fired the origin.
source: In our analysis, the height of the peak at the origin is linked to the number of cells that fired the origin, while the width of the peak indicates how far the fork is able to travel in HU.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the origin firing data based on the methodology used.

claim: The width of the peak indicates how far the fork is able to travel in HU.
source: In our analysis, the height of the peak at the origin is linked to the number of cells that fired the origin, while the width of the peak indicates how far the fork is able to travel in HU.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the origin firing data based on the methodology used.

claim: In sld3-A bob1 mutants, origin firing is not limited by availability of replication complex factors.
source: The fact that almost all origins fire demonstrates that, in sld3-A bob1 mutants, origin firing is not limited by availability of replication complex factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that almost all origins fire in sld3-A bob1 mutants.

claim: PP1 interacts with Rif1 to regulate origin firing through dephosphorylation of Mcm4 and possibly other substrates.
source: PP1 interacts with Rif1 to regulate origin firing through dephosphorylation of Mcm4 (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014) and possibly other substrates.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and speculation about other substrates.

claim: The level of Mcm4 phosphorylation did not correlate with the degree of origin activation.
source: While all three methods that we used to activate origins: rif1-pp1bs, ∆N-Dbf4 overexpression, and sld3-A bob1 mutations, resulted in increased Mcm4 phosphorylation, the level of Mcm4 phosphorylation did not correlate with the degree of origin activation.
evidence: This is based on the observation that different mutants have different levels of Mcm4 phosphorylation and origin activation.

claim: rif1∆ caused a higher increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation compared to both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and sld3-A bob1.
source: For example, rif1∆ caused a higher increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation compared to both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and sld3-A bob1 (Figures 2B and 3A); however, the activation of telomeric origins was much greater in both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and the sld3-A bob1 mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 3A.

claim: The activation of telomeric origins was much greater in both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and the sld3-A bob1 mutant compared to rif1∆.
source: For example, rif1∆ caused a higher increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation compared to both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and sld3-A bob1 (Figures 2B and 3A); however, the activation of telomeric origins was much greater in both ∆N-dbf4 Cdc7 overexpression and the sld3-A bob1 mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Figure 3C.

claim: Additional mechanisms, other than Mcm4 phosphorylation, likely also regulate dormant/telomeric origin firing.
source: This suggests that additional mechanisms, other than Mcm4 phosphorylation, likely also regulate dormant/telomeric origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Mcm4 phosphorylation does not correlate with origin activation.

claim: There are independent pathways that activate origins, and activation of multiple pathways can result in a higher fraction of cells firing dormant origins.
source: Our data supports the conclusion (Sheu et al., 2016; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010) that there are independent pathways that activate origins, and activation of multiple pathways can result in a higher fraction of cells firing dormant origins.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data and citations to Sheu et al., 2016 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Rif1 was first identified as a protein that bound to yeast telomeres through its interaction with Rap1.
source: Rif1 was first identified as a protein that bound to yeast telomeres through its interaction with Rap1 (Hardy et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hardy et al., 1992.

claim: Yeast telomeres were known to replicate late in S phase.
source: Yeast telomeres were known to replicate late in S phase, and when an early firing origin was relocated to a telomere, that origin then fired late (Ferguson et al., 1991; Ferguson and Fangman, 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 1991 and Ferguson and Fangman, 1992.

claim: The telomere location or telomeric chromatin causes inefficient origin firing.
source: This suggested that the telomere location or telomeric chromatin causes inefficient origin firing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that origins fire late when relocated to telomeres.

claim: The high local concentration of Rif1 at the telomere could dephosphorylate Mcm4 (and likely other Pre-RC components) and block local telomeric origin firing.
source: When Rif1 was discovered to regulate origin firing (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014; Peace et al., 2014), the solution to the late replication of telomeres appeared simple: the high local concentration of Rif1 at the telomere could dephosphorylate Mcm4 (and likely other Pre-RC components) and block local telomeric origin firing.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the known functions of Rif1.

claim: The model that high local concentration of Rif1 at the telomere blocks local telomeric origin firing is incomplete.
source: Our data, however, suggests this model is incomplete.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rif1-∆1322, which lacks telomere localization, does not activate telomeric origins.

claim: The rif1-∆1322 C-terminal truncation has been shown to block interaction of Rif1 with Rap1.
source: This rif1-∆1322 C-terminal truncation has been shown to block interaction of Rif1 with Rap1 (Hiraga et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2013) and cause loss of Rif1 telomeric localization (Hafner et al., 2018; Hiraga et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hiraga et al., 2014, Shi et al., 2013, Hafner et al., 2018, and Hiraga et al., 2018.

claim: The rif1-∆1322 C-terminal truncation causes loss of Rif1 telomeric localization.
source: This rif1-∆1322 C-terminal truncation has been shown to block interaction of Rif1 with Rap1 (Hiraga et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2013) and cause loss of Rif1 telomeric localization (Hafner et al., 2018; Hiraga et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hafner et al., 2018 and Hiraga et al., 2018.

claim: The lack of telomeric origin activation in the rif1-∆1322 mutant was surprising.
source: The lack of telomeric origin activation in the rif1-∆1322 mutant was surprising, as we expected that release of Rif1 from telomeres would release PP1 repression near telomeres.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' expectations and the surprising nature of the result.

claim: The C-terminal truncation termed rif1-∆C594 showed no effect on origin firing.
source: However, in support of our conclusions, the same C-terminal truncation, in their work termed rif1-∆C594, also showed no effect on origin firing (Hiraga et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hiraga et al., 2018.

claim: A two amino acid substitution in Rif1 that disrupts the Rif1-Rap1 binding, rif1RBM, showed some telomeric origin activation but not as significant as rif1∆.
source: In addition, a two amino acid substitution in Rif1 that disrupts the Rif1-Rap1 binding, rif1RBM, showed some telomeric origin activation but not as significant as rif1∆ (Hafner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hafner et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in the HOOK region of Rif1 are proposed to disrupt a mechanism for binding of Rif1 to DNA.
source: Mutations in the HOOK region of Rif1 are proposed to disrupt a mechanism for binding of Rif1 to DNA (Mattarocci et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2017.

claim: Mechanisms other than telomere localization of Rif1 may be responsible for repression of dormant/telomeric origins.
source: Together, the observations that rif1HOOK and rif1-∆1322 showed no increase in Mcm4 phosphorylation or dormant/telomeric origin activation suggest that mechanisms other than telomere localization of Rif1 may be responsible for repression of dormant/telomeric origins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rif1HOOK and rif1-∆1322 do not activate origins despite lacking telomere localization.

claim: Rif1 protein is conserved across a wide range of phyla.
source: Rif1 protein is conserved across a wide range of phyla and the role of Rif1 in replication timing is conserved from yeasts to Drosophila to humans (Cornacchia et al., 2012; Hayano et al., 2012; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cornacchia et al., 2012, Hayano et al., 2012, and Yamazaki et al., 2012.

claim: The role of Rif1 in replication timing is conserved from yeasts to Drosophila to humans.
source: Rif1 protein is conserved across a wide range of phyla and the role of Rif1 in replication timing is conserved from yeasts to Drosophila to humans (Cornacchia et al., 2012; Hayano et al., 2012; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cornacchia et al., 2012, Hayano et al., 2012, and Yamazaki et al., 2012.

claim: In mammals, the PP1 binding domain is located in the C terminal region of Rif1 rather than the N terminal region.
source: In mammals, while the PP1 binding domain is located in the C terminal region of Rif1 rather than the N terminal region, the interaction with PP1 still regulates late replicating regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of mammalian Rif1.

claim: In mammals, the interaction of Rif1 with PP1 still regulates late replicating regions.
source: In mammals, while the PP1 binding domain is located in the C terminal region of Rif1 rather than the N terminal region, the interaction with PP1 still regulates late replicating regions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of mammalian Rif1.

claim: Rif1 interacts with 53BP1 and the Shieldin complex to process double strand DNA breaks.
source: Rif1 interacts with 53BP1 and the Shieldin complex to process double strand DNA breaks, which affects the choice between homologous recombination and NHEJ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rif1 function in DNA repair.

claim: Rif1 affects the choice between homologous recombination and NHEJ.
source: Rif1 interacts with 53BP1 and the Shieldin complex to process double strand DNA breaks, which affects the choice between homologous recombination and NHEJ.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rif1 function in DNA repair.

claim: Loss of Rif1 has dramatic consequences for immunoglobulin rearrangements.
source: This choice plays a major role in immunoglobulin class switch recombination, and thus loss of Rif1 has dramatic consequences for immunoglobulin rearrangements (Callen et al., 2020; Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Silverman et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Callen et al., 2020, Chapman et al., 2013, Di Virgilio et al., 2013, and Silverman et al., 2004.

claim: Many Rif1 functions in homologous recombination and NHEJ are conserved across phyla.
source: Notably, while many of these Rif1 functions in homologous recombination and NHEJ are conserved across phyla (Fontana et al., 2018; Mattarocci et al., 2017) and (reviewed in Mattarocci et al., 2016), the role of Rif1 in telomere length regulation is not conserved in mammals (Buonomo et al., 2009; Silverman et al., 2004; Xu and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fontana et al., 2018, Mattarocci et al., 2017, and Mattarocci et al., 2016.

claim: The role of Rif1 in telomere length regulation is not conserved in mammals.
source: Notably, while many of these Rif1 functions in homologous recombination and NHEJ are conserved across phyla (Fontana et al., 2018; Mattarocci et al., 2017) and (reviewed in Mattarocci et al., 2016), the role of Rif1 in telomere length regulation is not conserved in mammals (Buonomo et al., 2009; Silverman et al., 2004; Xu and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buonomo et al., 2009, Silverman et al., 2004, and Xu and Blackburn, 2004.

claim: Rif1 regulates telomere length in a subset of species including S. pombe, where it can interact with the telomere binding protein Taz1.
source: Rif1 regulates telomere length in a subset of species including S. pombe (Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001), where it can interact with the telomere binding protein Taz1, and in C. glabrata (Castaño et al., 2005), where it interacts with Rap1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001.

claim: Rif1 regulates telomere length in C. glabrata, where it interacts with Rap1.
source: Rif1 regulates telomere length in a subset of species including S. pombe (Kanoh and Ishikawa, 2001), where it can interact with the telomere binding protein Taz1, and in C. glabrata (Castaño et al., 2005), where it interacts with Rap1.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Castaño et al., 2005.

claim: The ability to interact with telomere binding proteins may have been acquired in yeasts, which imparted a new role in telomere length regulation in these species.
source: This ability to interact with telomere binding proteins may have been acquired in yeasts, which imparted a new role in telomere length regulation in these species (reviewed in Mattarocci et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review by Mattarocci et al., 2016.

claim: In yeast engineered to have a chromosome with TTAGGG telomere repeat sequence, to which Rap1 does not bind, telomere equilibrium is maintained, and Rif1 deletion has no effect on the length of this telomere.
source: Remarkably, in yeast engineered to have a chromosome with TTAGGG telomere repeat sequence, to which Rap1 does not bind, telomere equilibrium is maintained, and Rif1 deletion has no effect on the length of this telomere (Brevet et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Brevet et al., 2003.

claim: Rif1 regulation of telomere length is specific to settings where Rif1 interacts with the telomere binding proteins.
source: These data suggest that Rif1 regulation of telomere length is specific to settings where Rif1 interacts with the telomere binding proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rif1 deletion has no effect on telomere length when Rap1 does not bind.

claim: The function of Rif1 in regulating origin firing is separable from its function in regulating telomere length.
source: We have shown that the function of Rif1 in regulating origin firing is separable from its function in regulating telomere length.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on multiple experimental approaches.

claim: PP1 recruitment is not necessary for telomere length regulation.
source: Further, PP1 recruitment is not necessary for telomere length regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing that PP1 binding mutants do not affect telomere length.

claim: While origin firing is not linked to telomere length, there is still significant evidence linking components of the replication machinery to telomere length.
source: However, while origin firing is not linked to telomere length, there is still significant evidence linking components of the replication machinery to telomere length (Dionne and Wellinger, 1998; Greider, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dionne and Wellinger, 1998 and Greider, 2016.

claim: Rif1 has been shown to block telomere elongation at clustered telomeres in late S phase.
source: Rif1 has been shown to block telomere elongation at clustered telomeres in late S phase, which may be a clue as to how it negatively regulates telomere addition (Gallardo et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gallardo et al., 2011.

claim: Interactions of Rif1 and Rif2 together with Rap1 form a 'molecular Velcro' that blocks telomerase access to the telomere.
source: Shi et al. suggest that interactions of Rif1 and Rif2 together with Rap1 form a 'molecular Velcro' that blocks telomerase access to the telomere (Shi et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2013.

claim: Both Rif1 and Rif2 block Tel1 recruitment to the telomeres.
source: Hirano et al. suggest that both Rif1 and Rif2 block Tel1 recruitment to the telomeres (Hirano et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hirano et al., 2009.

claim: Rif2 regulates Tel1 through catalytic modulation of the MRX complex.
source: Recent evidence indicates that Rif2 regulates Tel1 through catalytic modulation of the MRX complex (Hailemariam et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hailemariam et al., 2019.

claim: Rif1, like Rif2, might also have roles in telomere length regulation other than blocking Tel1 telomere localization.
source: This suggests a possibility that Rif1, like Rif2, might also have roles in telomere length regulation other than blocking Tel1 telomere localization.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Rif2 has multiple roles in telomere length regulation.

claim: The remarkable ability of distantly related species to maintain telomere length equilibrium argues for conserved core components of the regulatory process.
source: The remarkable ability of distantly related species to maintain telomere length equilibrium argues for conserved core components of the regulatory process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that telomere length equilibrium is maintained across species.

claim: Since yeast utilize defined sequence-specific origins while mammalian cells use a more stochastic mechanism to activate origins, perhaps it is not surprising that origin firing is not a major component of telomere length regulation.
source: Since yeast utilize defined sequence-specific origins while mammalian cells use a more stochastic mechanism to activate origins, perhaps it is not surprising that origin firing is not a major component of telomere length regulation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differences in origin firing mechanisms between yeast and mammals.

claim: It would be hard to imagine how these two different methods of origin activation would both lead to well-regulated telomere length distributions.
source: It would be hard to imagine how these two different methods of origin activation would both lead to well-regulated telomere length distributions.
evidence: This is speculation about the difficulty of reconciling different origin firing mechanisms with telomere length regulation.

claim: The identification of a telomerase-specific RPA protein, which binds single-stranded telomeric DNA at the replication fork and interacts with telomerase, offers one alternative mechanism linking replication to telomere elongation.
source: The identification of a telomerase-specific RPA protein (Gao et al., 2007), which binds single-stranded telomeric DNA at the replication fork and interacts with telomerase, offers one alternative mechanism linking replication to telomere elongation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2007.

claim: Rif1, in addition to its role in regulating origin firing, stabilizes stalled forks and regulates fork progression.
source: It is intriguing that Rif1, in addition to its role in regulating origin firing, stabilizes stalled forks and regulates fork progression (Mukherjee et al., 2019; Munden et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mukherjee et al., 2019, Munden et al., 2018, and Xu et al., 2010.

claim: We currently do not know how Rif1 regulates telomere elongation.
source: We currently do not know how Rif1 regulates telomere elongation; however, establishing that there are clear separable functions of Rif1 will allow dissection of the molecular mechanism of its telomere length regulation function.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Establishing that there are clear separable functions of Rif1 will allow dissection of the molecular mechanism of its telomere length regulation function.
source: We currently do not know how Rif1 regulates telomere elongation; however, establishing that there are clear separable functions of Rif1 will allow dissection of the molecular mechanism of its telomere length regulation function.
evidence: This is speculation about the future implications of the study's findings.
